claim: EU leaders at the special European Council in Brussels, which is due to end on Friday 27 November 2026, agree to provide Ukraine with €45bn of EU-borrowed financing for 2027 (the Commission's proposed loan), whether or not all 27 member states take part.

runs.reason:
**Base rate.** I start near 50%. In four comparable summit rounds, leaders reached a concrete deal twice: they deferred the €50bn Ukraine Facility in December 2023 and approved it in February 2024; they made a general financing commitment in October 2025 and agreed to the €90bn EU-borrowed loan in December 2025. That is a small set of precedents, not a statistical estimate. It shows that leaders can settle a large package at a summit, but also that a commitment to meet Ukraine’s needs often comes before agreement on the money. ([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/european-council/2023/12/14-15/))

**What moves this case.** **Up:** The Commission’s November 18 proposal gives leaders a concrete €45bn package to endorse, and the previous loan shows that opt-outs can coexist with EU borrowing. The criterion also allows a political endorsement before legislation is adopted. **Down:** Costa’s November 24 invitation explicitly presses for agreement on the long-term budget but is less definitive on Ukraine financing; the official agenda says leaders will take stock of the loan proposal. The November 25 reporting on ambassadors’ talks shows broad support for funding Ukraine, but unresolved positions on who pays and whether to link the loan to the wider budget. The separate €45bn allocation for 2027 published on November 25 is from the **existing** loan and does not count; in my judgment, it also gives leaders some room to defer the top-up. ([ec.europa.eu](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/api/files/document/print/en/ip_26_2454/IP_26_2454_EN.pdf))

**Window risk.** I put the chance that the summit itself does not take place in the window at about 1%. The larger risk is that it meets as scheduled but leaves the amount or guarantees for December. I allow roughly another 4 percentage points for a deal from this summit that is first announced after Friday’s cutoff: Costa expects a Friday finish, but the closest borrowing precedent was announced at 02:56 on the summit’s second calendar day. ([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/11/24/special-european-council-of-26-27-november-2026-invitation-letter-by-president-antonio-costa-to-the-members-of-the-european-council/))

**3. Strongest Reason the Outcome Might Fail**
Even though the criterion generously allows for an agreement with opt-outs or a text supported by fewer than 27 leaders (and even simple "endorses the Commission's proposal … and calls for its swift adoption" language), two major obstacles threaten a YES resolution by 23:59 on Friday 27 November:
1. **Deferral or "Take Note" Language:** Because the Commission only tabled the legal texts on 18 November—requiring an amendment to the current MFF Regulation (Article 312 TFEU, which requires unanimity)—and Germany is demanding that Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia, and Bulgaria not be given a free-rider exemption this time, leaders may only "take note" or hold an initial orientation debate and task ministers/Coreper to finalize the package for the regular mid-December European Council.
2. **Summit Overrun Past 23:59 Friday:** Because this summit's primary agenda item is the €1.78 trillion 2028–2034 MFF (with bilateral "confessionals" scheduled before reconvening at 27 to share conclusions), negotiations could easily drag past midnight on Friday night into Saturday 28 November, which automatically resolves the claim NO.

Balancing the high political will to signal support for Ukraine (and the low bar required by criterion (a) where endorsing the Commission's €45bn proposal and calling for its swift adoption suffices, even at fewer than 27) against the "take stock" framing, the German burden-sharing condition, the option to wait until the December summit, and the risk of a Friday night MFF summit overrun, I estimate a 52% probability of YES.

runs.reason:
The more likely outcome is no qualifying agreement inside the window. EU leaders do sometimes close Ukraine money in the room, but a first summit on a borrowing instrument tabled eight days earlier, with public refusals and an explicit link to the MFF, usually produces orientation language and a later decision point—not “agrees” or “endorses … and calls for swift adoption.”

Comparable cases point the same way. The €90bn Ukraine Support Loan was a December European Council product after a longer negotiation, not a decision at the first leaders’ discussion of the legal text. Multiannual budget deals almost never land in a single special summit. Late-October diplomatic framing already treated 26 November as the moment to discuss structure, with a year-end decision as the aim. That base rate for a qualifying political agreement at this meeting is low—on the order of one in four to one in three—before the Friday 23:59 cutoff.

What moves this case: the Commission’s 18 November package is a concrete EU-borrowed loan of up to €45bn (€25bn military, €20bn budget), so the number and the instrument exist and are on the agenda. Costa’s 24 November invitation puts Ukraine financing beside the MFF and says he aims to finish on Friday, which is a mild upward pull, and the criterion counts opt-outs and civilian-only participation. Against that, Merz has made an all-27 contribution a precondition for other financial decisions, including the budget; Fico has ruled Slovakia out and Babis has refused new guarantees; diplomats expected Bulgaria to join that group. Coreper on 24 November, reported on 25 November, found only “broad recognition” of the need and then disagreement on burden-sharing, interest treatment and whether Ukraine and the MFF move together, with end-2026 still the working deadline. Euronews reported on 19 November that the civilian-strand opt-in is unlikely to move the holdouts because the objection is political. A deal first announced after 23:59 Friday would also be NO.

The obvious failure mode for a deferral is a late bilateral compromise: all states “in,” some only on the civilian €20bn, with conclusions that endorse the Commission’s €45bn loan and call for swift adoption—language the criterion treats as YES—even if the MFF itself slips.
